title: Implicit weights
text:
Every estimator on this site can be written as a weighted average of simple comparisons, in the spirit of Goodman-Bacon (2021): \[
\hat\theta = \sum_c \omega_c\, \hat\delta_c .
\] The decomposition works at two levels. For the CS-type estimators, cohort effects are aggregated with weights \(\omega_g\) (level 1), and each cohort effect is computed against a comparison group with a given composition across matched-cohort labels (level 2). For TWFE, the weights are those of its \(2\times2\) comparisons, including comparisons that use already-treated units as controls.
The figures use the constant-effect pattern, where the true effect is 2 (dashed line). The vertical distance of a point from the line is the bias of that comparison, and its horizontal position is the weight it carries.

title: Inference
text:
The paper discusses three ways to compute standard errors for CM-CS. They differ in what they hold fixed:
The results below come from 300 Monte Carlo replications per design, with the overall ATT of CM-CS as the target. They describe the designs we simulate; they are not general results.

title: Inference
text:
Coverage

Constant effectDynamic, cohort-heterogeneous effect

























In these designs:

The default bootstrap is close to nominal when parallel trends hold unconditionally. It over-covers once trends depend on the covariates. Matched pairs co-move through their common trend, the within-pair covariance of the influence functions is negative, and ignoring it overstates the variance.
Matched-set clustering restores that covariance and is close to nominal coverage in every design (0.93–0.95).
The joint bootstrap repeats the matching in every replication and is also close to nominal (0.94–0.96). Its standard errors are within 7% of the clustered ones. So in these designs the variability from selecting the matches is largely captured by clustering on the realized pairs, as the theory for matching without replacement predicts.

Note



In the empirical application the paper reports the multiplier bootstrap clustered at the pre-displacement firm. A treated worker and the matched control are generally employed in different firms, so this construction also omits the within-pair covariance, which on its own makes it conservative in the designs above.

title: Simulation design
text:
Matching
Treated units are matched one-to-one, without replacement, to never-treated units by nearest neighbour on the standardized covariates \((X, Z)\) measured at \(g-3\), before any treatment-related dynamics. Matching proceeds sequentially in order of treatment: cohort 4 first, then 7, then 10, each drawing from the controls left by earlier cohorts. Every matched control therefore carries the label of the cohort it was matched to; never-treated units that are not matched are dropped.
The simulation uses greedy nearest-neighbour matching within each cohort. The paper’s application chooses the within-cohort assignment to minimize the total covariate discrepancy; the two coincide whenever matches are not contested.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
text:
The cohort-matched estimator rests on conditional parallel trends: within cohort \(g\), treated and never-treated units with the same pre-treatment covariates \(X^{(g)}_i\) would have followed the same untreated trend. Matching is one way to estimate the counterfactual trend under this assumption. The other is to keep all never-treated units and adjust for covariates directly, as in the doubly robust estimator of Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) with covariates \(X\) and \(Z\) (CS, covariates). It combines a linear outcome regression for the untreated trend with a propensity score for cohort membership.
Both routes target the same parameter. They differ in how they estimate the conditional expectation \(\mu^{g}_{\Delta,t}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1}\mid G=\infty, X^{(g)}=x]\): matching is nonparametric, while covariate adjustment relies on a working model.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
text:
The cohort-matched estimator rests on conditional parallel trends: within cohort \(g\), treated and never-treated units with the same pre-treatment covariates \(X^{(g)}_i\) would have followed the same untreated trend. Matching is one way to estimate the counterfactual trend under this assumption. The other is to keep all never-treated units and adjust for covariates directly, as in the doubly robust estimator of Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) with covariates \(X\) and \(Z\) (CS, covariates). It combines a linear outcome regression for the untreated trend with a propensity score for cohort membership.
Both routes target the same parameter. They differ in how they estimate the conditional expectation \(\mu^{g}_{\Delta,t}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1}\mid G=\infty, X^{(g)}=x]\): matching is nonparametric, while covariate adjustment relies on a working model.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
text:
An implementation identity
Take the matched sample and run CS with never-treated controls, conditioning on a set of dummies for the cohort each control was matched to. This reproduces CM-CS exactly: across all designs and patterns on this site, the two event-study estimates differ by at most 9e-16. With a saturated label, conditioning reduces to restricting each cohort to its own matched controls. This is an identity between two estimators, and a useful check on an implementation. It is not an identifying assumption: the label is produced by the matching in a given sample, not a characteristic of the population. The pooled matched estimator is the same regression without the label, and its bias is the cost of dropping it.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
text:
The cost of matching
One-to-one matching keeps one control per treated unit and discards the rest of the never-treated reservoir. When the covariate-adjusted model is correctly specified, that loss shows up as lower precision. With no trend, or a trend linear in \(X\) and \(Z\), CS with covariates has an RMSE about a fifth lower than CM-CS, and narrower replication bands. Once the working model is misspecified, its bias dominates and the ranking reverses.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
text:
Where covariate adjustment breaks down
Covariate adjustment needs the functional form of the trend to be right; matching does not.

Misspecified functional form. With an interaction (X × Z) or a quadratic (Quadratic in X) trend, the linear working model is wrong and the estimator is biased. Under the quadratic trend the bias is large, because the cohorts have little overlap in \(X\) and the linear model has to extrapolate across cohorts. Matching compares units with nearby covariate values and is unaffected here, because the never-treated reservoir is drawn to cover each cohort’s covariate distribution. If the control pool itself overlapped poorly with a cohort, matching would suffer too, through poorer matches.
Latent or moving trend drivers. Under a latent trend or drifting covariates both approaches are biased, and covariate adjustment more so in our designs.

Adding the right interactions or polynomial terms would repair the covariate-adjusted estimator, but only if the researcher knows which ones to add.

title: Matching vs. conditioning
section: Limits shared by matching and conditioning
text:
Limits shared by matching and conditioning
Matching and covariate adjustment use the same information: the observed pre-treatment covariates. In these designs, both can only correct for differences in untreated trends to the extent that the covariates reveal them. Neither can remove a bias from a trend driver that the covariates do not capture. What matching adds is robustness to the functional form, not to missing information.
The way to do better is to put more information into the matching variables. When the trend driver is a covariate that drifts after matching, matching on the covariate’s trajectory (its values at \(g-3\) and \(g-1\)) instead of a single snapshot recovers most of the bias:

title: Matched difference-in-differences with staggered treatment
text:
Matched difference-in-differences designs are the workhorse of the job-displacement literature: each displaced worker is matched to similar non-displaced workers before displacement, and effects are estimated on the matched sample. With staggered treatment, the matched controls of one cohort were chosen to resemble that cohort, not the others. Standard estimators applied to the pooled matched sample nonetheless compare each cohort with every cohort’s matched controls, which reintroduces the cross-cohort imbalance that matching was meant to remove.
This site collects the Monte Carlo evidence behind the estimator proposed in the paper. It compares three ways of estimating event-study effects on a matched sample:



Estimator
Comparison group for cohort \(g\)




TWFE, matched sample
All other units in the matched sample: own and other cohorts’ matched controls, not-yet-treated and already-treated units


CS, pooled matched sample
Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) with every matched control treated as never-treated


CM-CS (ours)
Only the never-treated units matched to cohort \(g\) itself

title: Matched difference-in-differences with staggered treatment
text:
Headline result





Mean bias of the event-study estimates over post-treatment periods, by source of the untreated trend (rows) and treatment-effect pattern (panels). 100 Monte Carlo replications.





Once untreated outcome trends depend on the matching covariates, applying CS or TWFE to the pooled matched sample is biased, even though every treated unit has a close match. Restricting each cohort to its own matched controls (CM-CS) removes this pooling bias. TWFE is additionally biased when effects differ across cohorts, even without any trend. A small bias remains for CM-CS only when trends are driven by characteristics that matching on the observed covariates cannot balance.

title: Matched difference-in-differences with staggered treatment
text:
Where to go next

Simulation design: the data-generating process, the trend designs and the matching scheme.
Results: event-study plots and bias tables for the three estimators, three treatment-effect patterns and eleven trend designs.
Matching vs. conditioning: when conditional parallel trends with covariate adjustment delivers the same answer, and where it breaks down.
Inference: coverage of the three variance constructions discussed in the paper.
Implicit weights: which \(2\times2\) comparisons each estimator averages over.

title: Results
text:
What CM-CS does not fix
CM-CS removes the pooling bias, but it is only as good as the matching itself:

Latent trend drivers (Latent U, Step in latent U). Matching on \(X\) and \(Z\) balances \(U\) only insofar as \(X\) and \(Z\) predict it, which leaves a small bias. All estimators are affected, CM-CS the least.
Covariates that move after matching (Drifting X). Units that look alike at \(g-3\) drift apart afterwards. Matching on the covariate trajectory rather than on a single snapshot largely removes this bias: see the conditioning page.
Cohort-specific slopes unrelated to \(X\) (Cohort-specific slopes). Here the matching covariates carry no information about the trend.
